### 2.1 CHiME Challenge (chime)

`data/benchmarks/audio-speech/chime.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-11-05 · last verified 2026-11-05

*Distant-microphone speech challenges since 2011: keywords in noise, meeting transcription, conversation enhancement.*

The CHiME challenges (Computational Hearing in Multisource Environments) and their workshops on speech processing in everyday environments, run since 2011. The first four editions scored recognition of single-speaker read speech in noise: keywords in Grid utterances mixed binaurally with recorded living-room noise (CHiME-1, 2011, as the PASCAL CHiME challenge), the same in harder mixing conditions or with a larger vocabulary (CHiME-2), and Wall Street Journal prompts read into a six-microphone tablet in cafés, street junctions, buses and pedestrian areas (CHiME-3 and CHiME-4). CHiME-5 and CHiME-6 moved to conversational speech recorded in twenty real dinner parties with Kinect arrays, and CHiME-6 added joint diarisation and recognition. Since CHiME-7 each edition is a set of independent tasks run by separate teams within the CHiME Steering Group's schedule: distant meeting transcription across scenarios and array types (DASR, 2023 and 2024), NOTSOFAR-1's single-device office meetings and MMCSG's smart-glasses conversations (2024), unsupervised domain adaptation for speech enhancement (UDASE, 2023), audio-visual transcription of parallel conversations (MCoRec, 2025-2026) and enhancement of conversations for hearing-aid and smart-glasses wearers (ECHI, 2025-2026), the last two ranked partly or wholly by listening tests. Teams receive training and development data, run their systems on evaluation audio without references and submit outputs that each task's organisers score. CHiME-10, announced in July 2026, has three enhancement and extraction tasks and opens on 4 February 2027.

#### chime · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary audio-speech/speech-recognition; secondary audio-speech/speaker-tasks; per_edition true · [S3][chime-s3]
  - why: Recognising distant, noisy speech is the series' one continuous line. CHiME-1 to CHiME-4 scored recognition of read speech in noise, CHiME-5 to CHiME-8 scored transcription of conversations, and CHiME-9's MCoRec scores per-speaker word error rate. Diarisation and speaker extraction are the secondary leaf, the scored half of several recent tasks.
  > The CHiME challenge series aims to advance robust automatic speech recognition (ASR) technology
- `capability` = perception · [S4][chime-s4]
  - why: Every task takes recorded audio and scores what was recovered from it, a transcript with speaker turns or an enhanced speech signal.
  > CHiME-6 targets the problem of distant microphone conversational speech recognition in everyday home environments.
- `capability` = distribution-shift-generalization · [S5][chime-s5]
  - why: CHiME-7 and CHiME-8 DASR rank one system over several meeting scenarios with different array topologies and forbid identifying the scenario, so the task stays fixed while the recording conditions move; CHiME-7 UDASE adapts enhancement trained on synthetic mixtures to real recordings.
  > Crucially, participants are forbidden to use automatic domain identification
- `evaluation_method` = reference-metric, domain-metric, classification-metric, human-crowd-eval, composite · [S6][chime-s6]
  - why: The latest recognition task combines two methods in its ranking metric; the latest enhancement task is ranked by human listeners.
  > Joint ASR-Clustering Error Rate (Primary Metric): Combined metric that weights transcription performance and clustering performance
- `designed_for_subjects` = task-specific-supervised-model · [S7][chime-s7]
  - why: Entrants build recognition, diarisation and enhancement pipelines trained for each task on its training data and the external data and pre-trained models its rules allow; since CHiME-7 those include self-supervised and large pre-trained speech models fine-tuned for the task.
  > Another departure from earlier CHiME iterations is that participants are allowed to use open-source pre-trained models and datasets.

#### chime · Task and evaluation

- `learned_entrant_evidence` = system \[withheld: it may name a person; see the entry file\] · [S11][chime-s11]
  > \[withheld: it may name a person; see the entry file\]

  - why: During a round the evaluation references are withheld, and the enhancement tasks' rankings rest on listening tests only the organisers run.
  > For the evaluation set, only the noisy Aria and HA audio and the rainbow passages were made public
- `task` = exists true; input far-field recordings of speech, from binaural and tablet-array recordings of read sentences in noise to multi-device array recordings of whole meetings and dinner parties, in recent tasks, smart-glasses and hearing-aid microphone arrays, 360-degree video, motion sensors and enrolment speech of the target talkers; output Per task, transcripts segmented by utterance with start and end times and a speaker label (CHiME-6 to CHiME-8), per-speaker transcripts with a conversation-cluster mapping (MCoRec), or enhanced speech signals, one stream per conversation partner in ECHI.; scoring Each task ranks on its own metric over its evaluation set; the CHiME-8 DASR ranking is tcpWER with a 5 s collar, computed per scenario and averaged over the four scenarios. · [S14][chime-s14]
  > In both tracks systems will be ranked according to scenario-wise macro time-constrained minimum permutation WER (tcpWER) with a collar of 5 s.
- `execution.reproducibility_tier` = not-independently-reproducible · [S13][chime-s13]
  - why: During a round only the organisers hold the evaluation references, and the enhancement tasks' official rankings come from listening tests the organisers run. After a round, recognition tasks whose references are released can be rescored with the official scripts.
  > a listening panel of 32 native English speakers with self-reported normal hearing was recruited
- `execution.harness` = Per task. CHiME-8 DASR's chime-utils (data generation, text normalisation and the official tcpWER, cpWER and DER scoring); MCoRec's and ECHI's evaluation scripts in their baseline repositories. · [S22][chime-s22]
  > the exact same scripts organizers will use for ranking CHiME-8 DASR submissions
- `aggregation_policy` = none-by-design · [S1][chime-s1]
  - why: Each task is ranked on its own metric and teams enter any subset of tasks; nothing combines the tasks.
  > Teams are responsible for managing the tasks, i.e., providing data and instructions, scoring submissions and results, etc.

**Open review checks** (11):

1. (field `versions`) Identity. One entry spans ten editions that change task type. CHiME-1 to CHiME-4 score recognition of single-speaker read speech in noise, CHiME-5 to CHiME-8 score transcription and diarisation of real conversations, and from CHiME-7 the tasks are proposed by separate teams; CHiME-9's ECHI and all three announced CHiME-10 tasks are enhancement or extraction, not recognition. The one-entry call follows the shared name and Steering Group, but CHiME-1 to CHiME-4 and the post-CHiME-7 task sets are far apart. · [S18][chime-s18]
   > The early CHiME challenges, up to CHiME-4, focused on single-speaker scenarios under controlled conditions with synthetic data.
2. (field `subsets`) NOTSOFAR-1 (Microsoft, its own name, paper, datasets and development leaderboard) and URGENT (a speech-enhancement challenge that is CHiME-10's Task 2) are hosted tasks with identities of their own. They are modelled as CHiME tasks here; either could be its own benchmark linked by lineage, which would need an id from the lead. · [S15][chime-s15]
   > we at Microsoft are excited to release two datasets for the benefit of the wider research community
3. (field `domain`) Overlap with dihard and voxsrc. CHiME-6 Track 2 is modelled on DIHARD II's multichannel diarisation track, and CHiME-6 to CHiME-8 report DER as DIHARD and the VoxSRC diarisation track do. The diarisation halves here are scored jointly with recognition (speaker-attributed WER), not as a diarisation ranking, so no lineage link is recorded; a correlates\_with link may suit once dihard is curated. · [S4][chime-s4]
   > Track 1 is a rerun of CHiME-5 and Track 2 is similar to the
4. (field `domain`) The primary domain is speech-recognition because recognition runs through CHiME-1 to CHiME-9. If CHiME-10 runs as announced, the series' current tasks are all enhancement and extraction, and a reviewer may prefer speaker-tasks or a speech-enhancement leaf as primary from then on. · [S26][chime-s26]
   > A unified speech enhancement system integrating universal speech enhancement, target speaker extraction, and acoustic echo cancellation for realistic conversational scenarios.
5. (field `domain.secondary`) Speech enhancement (UDASE, URGENT, the noise-suppression half of ECHI) has no audio-speech leaf; a bench tag-gap record proposes one. ECHI is given speaker-tasks because it extracts each partner's speech, which is speaker separation.
6. (field `evaluation_method`) execution\_mode is automated for the family, but UDASE and ECHI were ranked by listening panels (P.835 ratings and listener transcriptions from 32 native English speakers). The panels are tagged human-crowd-eval because no domain qualification is required; they are recruited and run by the organisers in a listening booth, not on a crowd platform. · [S23][chime-s23]
   > A panel of 32 native English speakers was recruited.
7. (field `activity`) activity round-scheduled rests on CHiME-10's dated opening (4 February 2027); its deadline and workshop are TBC, and between-rounds would hold if the opening slips. · [S10][chime-s10]
   > 4 Feb 2027 Challenge opening
8. (field `data.access`) data.access is train-open-test-held-out from the CHiME-9 round. Whether MCoRec's and ECHI's evaluation references are now released was not established (the ECHI dataset on Hugging Face has a test split behind its data use agreement, which was not requested). Old editions differ, CHiME-5's transcripts being open under CC BY-SA. · [S27][chime-s27]
   > Submission of a signed Data Use Agreement
9. (field `governance.submission_process`) publication-gated rests on MCoRec's rule that participants submit a system description; whether a report conditions the ranking in the other CHiME-8 and CHiME-9 tasks was not checked. · [S21][chime-s21]
   > Participants must submit a system description with details about their submitted system.
10. (field `governance.independence_flags`) Independence was not assessed. Industry runs or funds several tasks (Microsoft for NOTSOFAR-1, Meta and WS Audiology for ECHI, Meta's Aria glasses for MMCSG), and the entrant lists were not checked against the organisers' companies. · [S13][chime-s13]
   > This work was also supported by WS Audiology and Meta.
11. (field `released`) released is null. CHiME-1's schedule page and the overview papers of CHiME-1 to CHiME-4 (Computer Speech and Language and ICASSP/ASRU) were not read, so the editions before CHiME-7 carry no dates.

**Reviewer checklist** for `chime`:

- [ ] Identity and id: the name, aliases, id, paper and release date are right, and this is one benchmark, not a family or an edition of another
- [ ] Domain and capabilities: the primary and secondary subdomains, capabilities, evaluation methods and intended subjects fit, and no rejected term should have been kept
- [ ] Task and evaluation: the task, scoring, ground truth, entrants and harness read as the sources describe them
- [ ] Data and licence: access, refresh, provenance, sizes, subsets, contamination and licences match the sources
- [ ] Governance and independence: maintainer type, submission process, funding and independence flags are right
- [ ] Lifecycle and activity: lifecycle, activity, versions, editions and history are current
- [ ] Every open review check above is answered or resolved
- [ ] Nothing here would embarrass the catalogue in front of a specialist

### 2.2 Blizzard Challenge (blizzard-challenge)

`data/benchmarks/audio-speech/blizzard-challenge.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-10-14 · last verified 2026-10-14

*The text-to-speech challenge since 2005: every team builds a voice from the same data, and listeners judge the speech.*

The speech-synthesis community's shared evaluation, run since 2005. Each edition gives every team the same voice data and a set of test texts; teams build text-to-speech systems, synthesise the texts and submit the audio, and the organisers judge a selected subset in large listening tests. Listeners rate quality or naturalness on 5-point MOS scales and speaker similarity on MOS or MUSHRA-like 0-100 scales with a hidden natural reference; in 2023 intelligibility was the word error rate of listeners' transcriptions of semantically unpredictable sentences. The target speaker's natural speech is rated in the same tests. Results are reported per measure with pairwise Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, and no overall ranking is published. Editions have covered English, Mandarin and Shanghainese, Hindi, Tamil and Telugu, Spanish, French and Bildts. The 2023 edition, the eighteenth, was French: a 51-hour hub task and a 2-hour spoke task, with 18 and 14 teams. The 2025 edition was Bildts, a low-resource variety of the northern Netherlands: a 7-hour main task and a zero-shot task with a 10-second reference, with 7 and 5 teams, judged by native Bildts listeners and by Dutch and English-speaking listeners recruited on Prolific. The challenge now runs every two years beside ISCA's Speech Synthesis Workshop. The 2027 edition, accented zero-shot synthesis of spontaneous Brazilian and European Portuguese with about 790 hours of training speech, opened registration on 1 July 2026 and takes submissions until 12 April 2027. Each edition's submitted speech and listener scores are released afterwards through the University of Edinburgh's CSTR.

**Evidence** (45 quoted fields), by checklist area:

#### blizzard-challenge · Identity and id

- `self_description` · [S1][blizzard-challenge-s1]
  > Each edition provides shared datasets and evaluation protocols to enable direct comparison of synthesis approaches
- `released` = null · [S2][blizzard-challenge-s2]
  > In January of 2005, we released two further databases and a set of 50 utterance texts from each of five genres

#### blizzard-challenge · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary audio-speech/speech-synthesis; secondary language/low-resource-languages; per_edition true · [S2][blizzard-challenge-s2]
  - why: Every edition scores speech that the entrants synthesised from text, as listeners hear it. The 2025 edition was built around Bildts, a variety with no automatic metrics or pretrained models, which is the secondary leaf's case; it applies to that edition, not to the series.
  > Their resulting synthesized utterances were then presented to three groups of listeners: speech experts, volunteers, and US English-speaking undergraduates
- `capability` = generation-fidelity · [S1][blizzard-challenge-s1]
  - why: Similarity tests ask listeners how close the synthetic voice is to the target speaker, against a hidden natural reference, and the 2025 zero-shot task scored whether a voice built from a 10-second reference kept the speaker's identity.
  > This task explored whether systems could preserve both speaker identity and Bildts language characteristics with a short reference audio
- `capability` = communication · [S3][blizzard-challenge-s3]
  - why: Intelligibility is scored on what the listener understood. In 2023 listeners wrote down the semantically unpredictable sentences they heard, and the word error rate of their transcriptions is the score. 2025 replaced it with word-level issue marking (see review\_checks).
  > Test 3 measured Word Error Rate in a transcription task of SUS stimuli
- `evaluation_method` = human-crowd-eval, reference-metric · [S1][blizzard-challenge-s1]
  - why: Every score comes from listeners recruited without a domain qualification. In 2025 they were native Bildts speakers recruited locally and Prolific workers screened on first language or English fluency; in 2023, French-native Prolific workers and online volunteers. A language screen is not a domain qualification under the term's test. reference-metric is 2023's word error rate of listeners' transcriptions against the sentence text (see review\_checks).
  > Listeners were recruited via Prolific. As screening criterion, we imposed Dutch to be the first and primary language
- `designed_for_subjects` = generative-media-model · [S3][blizzard-challenge-s3]
  - why: Entrants are text-to-speech systems, and every score is a property of the speech they generate. The 2023 and 2025 entrants were all neural (FastSpeech-, Tacotron-, flow- and diffusion-based); the sources read do not describe the earlier editions' unit-selection and statistical systems.
  > All teams used neural-based systems

Considered and rejected:

- `capability` not `sample-efficiency` · [S1][blizzard-challenge-s1]
  - why: The target speaker's data is fixed (2 hours in 2023's spoke task, 10 seconds in 2025's zero-shot task), but external data is unrestricted in those tasks, so no total budget is scored.
  > BS1 had no constraints on external data or model usage
- `evaluation_method` not `human-expert-eval` · [S2][blizzard-challenge-s2]
  - why: Speech experts take part as self-identified volunteers and their ratings are pooled with the rest; no edition read recruits listeners for a professional credential.
  > Their resulting synthesized utterances were then presented to three groups of listeners: speech experts, volunteers, and US English-speaking undergraduates
- `evaluation_method` not `entrant-relative-ranking` · [S1][blizzard-challenge-s1]
  - why: Each system's scores are its own listeners' ratings, compared pair by pair for significance; the organisers publish no rank or pool-fitted scale and say the figures' order is not a ranking.
  > The order in each figure cannot be interpreted as the system ranking, as it does not reflect the results of the pairwise comparisons

#### blizzard-challenge · Task and evaluation

- `learned_entrant_evidence` = system Idiap kNN-TTS (Blizzard Challenge 2025) · [S5][blizzard-challenge-s5]
  > Idiap kNN-TTS System for the Blizzard Challenge 2025
- `learned_entrant_evidence` = system NRCC (Blizzard Challenge 2025) · [S5][blizzard-challenge-s5]
  > The NRCC Submission to the Blizzard Challenge 2025
- `reproducible_by_third_party` = true · [S6][blizzard-challenge-s6]
  - why: Each edition's submitted speech, test material and listener scores are released, and the 2025 listening-test recipes are public, so anyone can rerun a test with a subset of the systems and a new one. A rerun's listeners and pool differ, so its numbers are not the edition's.
  > Re-running the challenge, such as with a subset of the systems plus a new system
- `task` = exists true; input the edition's voice data, hours of one speaker's recorded speech with transcripts, or in zero-shot tasks a short reference utterance of an unseen target speaker, the test texts, given as orthographic text (sentences, and in 2025 also paragraphs and whole texts); output Synthetic speech for every test text in the target speaker's voice, submitted as audio files for the organisers' listening tests.; scoring Listeners rate a selected subset per measure (MOS for quality or naturalness, MOS or MUSHRA-like similarity with a hidden natural reference, transcription WER for intelligibility in 2023, Bildts-likeness, appropriateness and word-level issues in 2025), and systems are compared per measure by pairwise Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. No overall ranking. · [S1][blizzard-challenge-s1]
  > For most measures, we used Wilcoxon signed-rank tests for pairwise system comparisons
- `execution.compute_tier` = human-panel · [S3][blizzard-challenge-s3]
  - why: The cost of a score is the listeners' paid time; each team's own training and synthesis cost varies with its system.
  > Listeners were compensated at a rate of 10£/ hour
- `execution.reproducibility_tier` = requires-human-raters · [S1][blizzard-challenge-s1]

### 2.3 ASVspoof (asvspoof)

`data/benchmarks/audio-speech/asvspoof.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-11-05 · last verified 2026-11-05

*Community challenge on detecting spoofed and deepfake speech and on spoofing-robust speaker verification, 2015-2024.*

The Automatic Speaker Verification Spoofing and Countermeasures Challenge, a community-led series begun after an Interspeech special session in 2013 and run in 2015, 2017, 2019, 2021 and 2024 (ASVspoof 5) by an organising committee from EURECOM, the National Institute of Informatics, the University of Eastern Finland and others. Participants build countermeasures that give each speech utterance a score for bona fide against spoofed speech, or spoofing-robust speaker verification systems that must accept only the claimed speaker's genuine speech. 2015 scored detection of speech synthesis and voice conversion; 2017 replay attacks; 2019 logical access (synthesis and conversion, with neural attacks) and simulated physical access (replay); 2021 logical access over telephony channels, physical access in real rooms and a new speech deepfake task over compressed audio. ASVspoof 5 moved to crowdsourced data from about 2,000 speakers with 32 attack algorithms, adversarial attacks and codecs, and to two tracks (stand-alone detection; spoofing-robust ASV), each with closed and open training conditions. Evaluation audio is released without keys and scored by the organisers, who rank by a detection cost (t-DCF from 2019; minDCF and a-DCF in ASVspoof 5); the keys are released afterwards. ASVspoof 5 drew 53 teams.

#### asvspoof · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary audio-speech/speaker-tasks · [S1][asvspoof-s1]
  - why: The series exists to protect automatic speaker verification. Every edition scores countermeasures against spoofed speech presented to a speaker verifier, the tandem metric from 2019 scores them with a fixed ASV system, and ASVspoof 5's Track 2 scores spoofing-robust speaker verification itself, which the leaf's 'verifying' names. Stand-alone detection (Track 1, the 2021 DF task) decides nothing about who is speaking and has no leaf; that gap is logged.
  > ASVspoof is centred around the challenges to design: (1) spoofing-robust automatic speaker verification (SASV) solutions; (2) stand-alone speech deepfake detectors.
- `capability` = perception · [S3][asvspoof-s3]
  - why: The input is a raw speech waveform and the score measures what was recovered from it, whether the speech is bona fide and, in Track 2, whether it is the target speaker's.
  > Track 1 involves a stand-alone spoof/deepfake speech detection task (bonafide versus spoof)
- `capability` = adversarial-robustness · [S3][asvspoof-s3]
  - why: The attacks are made by an adversary to defeat the system. In ASVspoof 5 the data contributors tuned their attacks against surrogate countermeasure and ASV systems, and seven of the sixteen evaluation attacks are adversarial attacks aimed at the CM, the ASV system or both; the score is the detector's resistance.
  > Among the 16 attacks in the evaluation set, seven are adversarial attacks designed to manipulate the CM, ASV system, or both.
- `capability` = distribution-shift-generalization · [S3][asvspoof-s3]
  - why: Beyond the attacks (which are adversarial), the evaluation sets move the channel deliberately and report it as conditions of their own. ASVspoof 5 encodes part of the evaluation set only with MP3, Opus, AMR, Speex, M4A, Encodec and simulated telephony; the 2021 LA task added transmission channels, the DF task compression, and the PA task real rooms after simulated training data. The bona fide-or-spoof task is unchanged.
  > a portion of bona fide and spoofed utterances in only the evaluation set are encoded or compressed
- `evaluation_method` = domain-metric, classification-metric · [S3][asvspoof-s3]
  - why: ASVspoof 5 moved Track 1 from EER to a detection cost function, and Track 2 ranks by the minimum a-DCF; EER is kept for continuity with earlier editions.
  > the detection cost function (DCF) \[49\] metric was adopted for performance evaluation
- `designed_for_subjects` = task-specific-supervised-model · [S3][asvspoof-s3]
  - why: Entrants are countermeasures and spoofing-robust speaker verification systems trained for the task, on the edition's training partition alone in the closed condition; the open condition admits pretrained speech foundation models, fine-tuned and scored as trained systems.
  > For the open condition, wav2vec2 and WavLM models are utilised by all the top submissions.

#### asvspoof · Task and evaluation

- `learned_entrant_evidence` = system The top ASVspoof 5 open-condition submissions (wav2vec2 and WavLM front-ends with neural back-ends) · [S3][asvspoof-s3]
  > For the open condition, wav2vec2 and WavLM models are utilised by all the top submissions.
- `learned_entrant_evidence` = system A curriculum-trained speech deepfake detector, scored on ASVspoof 2021 and ASVspoof 5 · [S4][asvspoof-s4]
  > reducing overall EER from 3.04% to 1.48% on ASVspoof 2021, from 25.43% to 21.04% on ASVspoof 5

- `task` = exists true; input one speech utterance (countermeasure tasks; ASVspoof 5 Track 1), a test utterance with enrolment utterances of a claimed target speaker (2019-2021 LA and PA with the organisers' ASV system; ASVspoof 5 Track 2); output A single real-valued score per utterance or trial, higher for bona fide (or for the target speaker), each item scored independently of the others.; scoring The organisers set the decisions and compute the edition's metrics from the score files. 2015 and 2017 by EER; 2019 and 2021 by min t-DCF with EER (EER alone for 2021 DF); ASVspoof 5 Track 1 by minDCF with actDCF, Cllr and EER, Track 2 by min a-DCF with min t-DCF and t-EER. **Open review checks** (9):

1. (field `domain.primary`) domain.primary is speaker-tasks, which fits Track 2 and the tandem LA and PA tasks but not stand-alone detection (2015, 2017, 2021 DF, Track 1), which decides nothing about who is speaking. No leaf anywhere covers spoofing or deepfake detection, and there is no security family; a missing-term gap is logged proposing a detection leaf. Should the primary instead wait for that leaf? · [S3][asvspoof-s3]
   > There are two tasks, namely the design of stand-alone CMs (spoof/deepfake speech detectors) and of spoofing-robust ASV systems.
2. (field `activity`) activity between-rounds rests on the absence of any announced edition and on no standing board being shown. The editions' CodaLab competitions (2021, ASVspoof 5) were not read; if any keeps a post-evaluation phase open, activity is leaderboard-live-no-round. With editions 'previously-biennial' and none in 2026, a reviewer may judge the series closed instead. · [S1][asvspoof-s1]
   > ASVspoof 5 is the fifth edition in a series of previously-biennial, competitive challenges
3. (field `governance.maintainer_type`) maintainer\_type community-collective or conference-workshop. Each edition is held with Interspeech or as its satellite and the committee grew from four to thirteen, but a core from EURECOM, NII and UEF runs every edition.
4. (field `versions`) The entry is the five-edition series, with LA, PA and DF and ASVspoof 5's tracks as subsets. ASVspoof 2019 LA is so widely used as a standing training and test set that it could be argued as its own entry; it is the same maintainer's frozen edition, which the counting rule keeps as a version. The SASV 2022 challenge (spoofing-aware speaker verification, built on ASVspoof 2019 LA, with overlapping organisers) is not covered and would be its own entry or a lineage variant.
5. (field `capability`) adversarial-robustness is tagged because spoofing attacks are made by an adversary and ASVspoof 5's attacks were tuned against surrogate detectors, with seven adversarial attacks; distribution-shift-generalization rests on the codec and channel conditions only, since the vocabulary sends adversarially made shifts to adversarial-robustness. · [S1][asvspoof-s1]
   > Spoofing/deepfake attacks are expected to be more adversarial than in previous editions of ASVspoof and to fool both ASV and CM surrogate subsystems.
6. (field `evaluation_method`) calibration-uncertainty and uncertainty-calibration-score were rejected because Cllr and actDCF are reported but not ranked. The organisers say calibration-sensitive metrics may become primary in future editions. · [S3][asvspoof-s3]
   > Note, however, that any order-preserving score calibration does not affect the primary minDCF metric.
7. (field `data.access`) data.access fully-open assumes the 2015, 2017 and 2019 DataShare records serve the data and keys without registration; they were not read, and the 2015 page describes a username and password scheme from the challenge period. dataset\_licence ODC-By-1.0 is read from the ASVspoof 5 record and the 2021 page only. · [S7][asvspoof-s7]
   > 5th June: Database Release via Edinburgh DataShare.
8. (field `governance.independence_flags`) independence was not assessed. The funders appear only as logos, team identities are withheld, and industry organisers (Pindrop, Microsoft) could have entered. · [S3][asvspoof-s3]
   > As per ASVspoof Challenge policy, neither the team name nor the names of team members can be revealed.
9. (field `versions`) The edition released dates are each edition's first data release as its own page dates it (2016-12-23 for 2017 and 2018-12-19 for 2019 from the schedules), and ASVspoof 5's is Phase 2's opening (Phase 1 opened on 1 July 2023 for data contributors). The 2021 date is the Zenodo release of 28 May 2021. · [S5][asvspoof-s5]
   > Phase 1 - registration opens July 1, 2023

### 2.4 Deep Noise Suppression Challenge (dns-challenge)

`data/benchmarks/audio-speech/dns-challenge.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-11-05 · last verified 2026-11-18

*Microsoft's five-round speech enhancement challenge (2020-2023), ranked by crowdsourced listening tests.*

Microsoft's Deep Noise Suppression Challenge, five rounds held at Interspeech 2020, ICASSP 2021, Interspeech 2021, ICASSP 2022 and ICASSP 2023. Entrants build single-channel speech enhancement models that remove background noise and, in later rounds, reverberation and interfering talkers, and submit the enhanced clips of a blind test set that is released a few days before the deadline. Microsoft scores them with its own crowdsourced listening tests: ITU-T P.808 absolute category rating MOS in 2020 and early 2021, then P.835 ratings of speech signal (SIG), background noise (BAK) and overall quality (OVRL), with a personalised variant that plays the primary talker's enrolment speech to the raters. From 2022 the rank is a challenge score that weights P.835 OVRL and word accuracy from a speech recogniser equally. Each round brought new real recordings collected through crowdsourcing (with synthetic mixtures beside them in 2020) and its own tracks: real-time and non-real-time (2020), real-time and personalised (ICASSP 2021), wideband and fullband (Interspeech 2021), non-personalised and personalised fullband (2022), and headset and speakerphone (2023). Microsoft open-sourced the training corpora and synthesiser, the test sets, the P.808 and P.835 toolkits and the DNSMOS quality predictors, and the 2020 test sets in particular remain a common evaluation set for speech enhancement papers, now usually scored with DNSMOS rather than listeners.

**Evidence** (50 quoted fields), by checklist area:

#### dns-challenge · Identity and id

- `self_description` · [S1][dns-challenge-s1]
  > DNS challenges were organized during 2019-2023 to stimulate research in deep speech enhancement
- `release_venue` = Interspeech 2020 · [S1][dns-challenge-s1]
  > Previous DNS challenges were organized at INTERSPEECH 2020, ICASSP 2021, INTERSPEECH 2021, and ICASSP 2022.

#### dns-challenge · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary audio-speech/speaker-tasks · [S1][dns-challenge-s1]
  - why: The task is speech enhancement, which has no audio-speech leaf (logged with bench tag-gap). The nearest leaf is speaker-tasks, whose definition includes separating speakers from audio. Every round separates one talker's speech from noise and reverberation, and the personalised tracks (from ICASSP 2021) and both 2023 tracks keep the primary talker, given by enrolment speech, while suppressing neighbouring talkers. The score is on the enhanced audio itself.
  > The goal is to enhance audio signal and preserve the primary talker while suppressing the neighboring talkers, noise, and reverberation.
- `capability` = perception · [S2][dns-challenge-s2]
  - why: The input is raw noisy speech audio, and the score measures how well the target speech was recovered from it, as listeners hear it.
  > Speech Enhancement aimed to maximize the subjective (perceptual) quality of the enhanced speech
- `capability` = distribution-shift-generalization · [S2][dns-challenge-s2]
  - why: Training data is synthesised by mixing clean speech with noise, and the rounds are ranked on real recordings made on unseen devices and in unseen rooms, which the organisers chose because models that do well on synthetic mixtures fail on real recordings. The 2020 results report synthetic, synthetic-reverberant and real clips as separate columns.
  > While the performance is good on the synthetic test set, often the model performance degrades significantly on real recordings.
- `evaluation_method` = human-crowd-eval, model-derived-metric, composite · [S1][dns-challenge-s1]
  - why: Every round is ranked by listeners recruited on Amazon Mechanical Turk and screened by hearing and environment tests, not by domain qualification (P.808 MOS in 2020 and ICASSP 2021; P.835 SIG, BAK and OVRL from Interspeech 2021). From 2022, word accuracy is computed by Microsoft's speech recogniser (Azure Speech Recognition) against the organisers' transcripts, a scoring model whose version is part of the result, and the challenge score averages the rescaled P.835 OVRL with it, which is composite.
  > Final score = 0.5\[WAcc + 0.25(OVRL − 1)\]
- `designed_for_subjects` = task-specific-supervised-model · [S3][dns-challenge-s3]
  - why: Entrants are noise suppression networks trained on noisy-clean pairs, the challenge's synthesiser output or their own, and scored as trained; the subjects vocabulary names denoising networks as this term, although they output audio.
  > noisyspeech\_synthesizer\_singleprocess.py\*\* - is used to synthesize noisy-clean speech pairs for training purposes

Considered and rejected:

- `evaluation_method` not `human-expert-eval` · [S2][dns-challenge-s2]
  - why: Raters are crowd workers qualified by a hearing and environment test, not by a professional credential.
  > Raters are first qualified using a hearing and environmental test before they can start rating clips.

#### dns-challenge · Task and evaluation

- `learned_entrant_evidence` = system NSNet2, the organisers' non-personalised baseline (ICASSP 2022) · [S6][dns-challenge-s6]
  > We trained NSNet2 \[3, 15\] on a subset of the fullband nonpersonalized training dataset to obtain the baseline.
- `learned_entrant_evidence` = system LL-SDR, a token-based enhancement model, on the DNS Challenge 2020 test sets (DNSMOS) · [S4][dns-challenge-s4]
  > LL-SDR (Ours) 3.27 3.55 4.08 3.39 3.62 4.16 3.16 3.45 4.05
- `reproducible_by_third_party` = false · [S1][dns-challenge-s1]
  - why: The listening tests can be rerun with the open toolkits on the released blind sets, but the 2022-2023 score also needs the organisers' unreleased blind-set transcripts and Microsoft's Azure speech recogniser, computed internally. The 2020-2021 MOS-only rankings are reproducible in method, though a rerun's raters differ.
  > We computed WAcc results internally.
- `task` = exists true; input a noisy, possibly reverberant single-channel speech clip (16 kHz in 2020-2021, 48 kHz fullband from Interspeech 2021's fullband track on), for personalised models, enrolment speech of the primary talker (2.5 minutes in 2022, 10-30 s in 2023); output The enhanced clip, with background noise, reverberation and (in personalised and 2023 tracks) neighbouring talkers suppressed, produced in real time under the round's latency and compute limits (2020 also had a non-real-time track).; scoring Crowdsourced listening tests on the enhanced blind set, P.808 MOS (2020, ICASSP 2021) or P.835 SIG, BAK and OVRL (from Interspeech 2021, personalised in 2022-2023); from 2022 the challenge score is 0.5 x (WAcc + (OVRL - 1) / 4). ANOVA separates the top teams; ties go to the lower-complexity model. · [S2][dns-challenge-s2]
  > Three winners were selected from each track based on the subjective speech quality evaluated on the blind test set using ITU-T P.808 framework.
- `execution.compute_tier` = human-panel · [S8][dns-challenge-s8]
  - why: The cost of a score is paid crowd raters on Amazon Mechanical Turk; each team's own training and inference cost varies with its model.
  > We provide an open-source implementation of the ITU-T Rec. P.808 that runs on the Amazon Mechanical Turk platform.
- `execution.reproducibility_tier` = requires-human-raters · [S9][dns-challenge-s9]
  - why: Every round's ranking needs crowd raters; the P.835 toolkit used from Interspeech 2021 was validated against a laboratory test and in a round-robin.
  > Finally, we used our implementation in the INTERSPEECH 2021 Deep Noise Suppression Challenge as the primary evaluation metric
- `execution.harness` = The open-source P.808 and P.835 crowdsourcing toolkits (github.com/microsoft/P.808), the repository's WAcc script and DNSMOS (DNSMOS/dnsmos\_local.py); they run a listening test or estimate one, but the official score is the organisers' crowd ratings and internal WAcc. · [S10][dns-challenge-s10]
  > Use the \*\*dnsmos\_local.py\*\* script.
- `execution.submission_channel` · [S1][dns-challenge-s1]
  > Registration and submission of enhanced clips was done through CMT site
- `aggregation_policy` = none-by-design · [S1][dns-challenge-s1]
  - why: Each track has its own subjective evaluation, ranking and winners, and nothing combines the tracks or the rounds. Within a 2022-2023 track the challenge score is an official combination of OVRL and WAcc (see evaluation\_method).
  > (vi) Track-1 and Track-2 has their separate subjective evaluations

**Open review checks** (12):

1. (field `domain`) Domain. Speech enhancement has no audio-speech leaf (logged with bench tag-gap, proposing audio-speech/speech-enhancement). speaker-tasks was chosen for its separating clause and the personalised, talker-suppressing tracks; speech-synthesis (speech output scored by listener MOS) was the runner-up. The 2020-2021 non-personalised tracks separate speech from noise, not speakers from each other.
2. (field `lifecycle`) lifecycle active rests on one July 2026 paper that scores the 2020 test sets with DNSMOS, not with the challenge's listening tests. Whether a DNSMOS score on a released test set counts as results produced against this instrument, rather than against the derived DNSMOS protocol, decides between active and mature. · [S4][dns-challenge-s4]
   > We evaluate speech quality using DNSMOS \[27\].
3. (field `activity`) activity closed. No source announces the series' end; it rests on the 2023 paper's 'organized during 2019-2023', the fifth round's programme dates and the absence of later rounds. Microsoft's ICASSP 2024 grand challenges were not read; if a later round carries the DNS name, the series is not closed. · [S1][dns-challenge-s1]
   > DNS challenges were organized during 2019-2023 to stimulate research in deep speech enhancement
4. (field `data.access`) data.access train-open-test-held-out is judged on the fifth round, whose blind-set transcripts were not released; read on the 2020 test sets that later papers use, which have clean references and no withheld labels, the entry would be fully-open. The blind archives themselves were not downloaded.
5. (field `ground_truth_source`) ground\_truth\_source held-out-labels rests on the 2022-2023 WAcc half; the P.808 and P.835 ratings that ranked 2020-2021, and half the later score, are panel judgements with no stored answer (none).
6. (field `evaluation_method`) evaluation\_method model-derived-metric and composite rest on the 2022-2023 rounds only; 2020-2021 were P.808 or P.835 MOS alone. Whether family tags should rest on two of five rounds. · [S6][dns-challenge-s6]
   > The motivation to add WAcc as an evaluation metric stems from the fact that several models from past challenges had noticeable WAcc degradation
7. (field `versions`) Identity. One family entry with five rounds as editions and their tracks as subsets. DNSMOS and DNSMOS P.835, which Microsoft released as separate metrics and which most later papers report on the 2020 test sets, are treated as the scorer (harness), not as their own benchmarks; a reviewer may want the 2020 test set, as used with DNSMOS, as a separate entry linked by lineage.
8. (field `data.contamination_risk`) contamination\_risk medium rests on PTDB-TUG appearing both as the 2020 synthetic test clips' clean speech and among the fifth round's training corpora; which rounds' training data first included it, and whether the test speakers' sentences are in it, was not checked. · [S2][dns-challenge-s2]
   > For synthetic test clips, we used Graz University
9. (field `governance.independence_flags`) independence\_flags is empty. Prizes existed in 2020, but no source names the funder; the 2023 page's Results and Organizers tabs did not render in the served HTML and were not read. · [S2][dns-challenge-s2]
   > Hence, the three prizes can be easily picked based on speech quality.
10. (field `governance.submission_process`) publication-gated rests on the 2022 disqualifications; the 2020 and 2021 rules were not read.
11. (field `reproducible_by_third_party`) reproducible\_by\_third\_party false follows the 2022-2023 score's internal WAcc; the 2020-2021 rankings used only crowd MOS, which the open toolkits can rerun on the released blind sets.
12. (field `evaluation_method`) The ICASSP 2021 round's scoring is read as P.808 MOS from the Interspeech 2021 abstract's account of the earlier rounds (it names 'INTERSPEECH and ICASSP 2020', apparently meaning 2020 and ICASSP 2021) and the P.835 paper's statement that P.835 was first used in Interspeech 2021; the ICASSP 2021 paper's own abstract says only 'subjective tests', and its PDF was not read. · [S12][dns-challenge-s12]
   > We also open-sourced a subjective evaluation framework based on ITU-T standard P.808, which was also used to evaluate participants of the challenge.

**Reviewer checklist** for `dns-challenge`:

- [ ] Identity and id: the name, aliases, id, paper and release date are right, and this is one benchmark, not a family or an edition of another
- [ ] Domain and capabilities: the primary and secondary subdomains, capabilities, evaluation methods and intended subjects fit, and no rejected term should have been kept
- [ ] Task and evaluation: the task, scoring, ground truth, entrants and harness read as the sources describe them
- [ ] Data and licence: access, refresh, provenance, sizes, subsets, contamination and licences match the sources
- [ ] Governance and independence: maintainer type, submission process, funding and independence flags are right
- [ ] Lifecycle and activity: lifecycle, activity, versions, editions and history are current
- [ ] Every open review check above is answered or resolved
- [ ] Nothing here would embarrass the catalogue in front of a specialist

### 2.5 IWSLT Evaluation Campaign (iwslt)

`data/benchmarks/audio-speech/iwslt.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-10-14 · last verified 2026-10-14

*IWSLT's yearly speech-translation shared tasks since 2004: offline, simultaneous, low-resource, subtitling and more.*

The evaluation campaign of the International Conference on Spoken Language Translation (IWSLT), run every year since 2004 under SIGSLT, the ACL special interest group. Each edition is a set of shared tasks: organisers release training and development data and test audio, teams submit system outputs before the conference, and the organisers score them and report the results in a findings paper in the ACL Anthology. The 2026 edition, the 23rd, had ten tasks: offline, low-resource, simultaneous and subtitling speech translation, model compression, Indic and African/Celtic speech-to-speech translation, cross-lingual voice cloning, instruction following for speech language models, and quality estimation for speech translation. The offline track, the oldest, ranks submissions by COMET against withheld reference translations after automatic resegmentation, reports BLEURT, BLEU, TER and characTER beside it, and has professional translators rate each team's primary run by direct assessment. Systems are entered under constrained, constrained-with-LLM and unconstrained data conditions. IWSLT 2027 has added year-round leaderboards on the evaluation server for the offline, compression and instruction-following tracks.

**Evidence** (53 quoted fields), by checklist area:

#### iwslt · Identity and id

- `self_description` · [S1][iwslt-s1]
  > The International Conference on Spoken Language Translation (IWSLT) is an annual scientific conference, associated with shared tasks on spoken language translation
- `released` = 2004-09-30 · [S2][iwslt-s2]
  > IWSLT 2004, 30 Sep.-01 Oct. 2004 - Kyoto, Japan

#### iwslt · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary audio-speech/speech-translation; secondary audio-speech/speech-recognition, audio-speech/speech-synthesis, language/low-resource-languages, multimodal/audio-language; per_edition true · [S1][iwslt-s1]
  - why: Every shared task takes speech as input, and the campaign's purpose is translating it; the longest-running track scores text translations of recorded speech.
  > associated with shared tasks on spoken language translation
- `capability` = generation-fidelity · [S3][iwslt-s3]
  - why: The offline track's ranking is COMET similarity to the reference translations, and professional translators rate each primary run against the source audio; other tracks score BLEU, chrF++, SubER or character error rate against references.
  > produce translations similar to the target-language references in the test sets
- `capability` = perception · [S4][iwslt-s4]
  - why: Every track starts from raw speech, much of it long-form audio with overlapping speakers, accents and noise, and what is scored is the content recovered from it.
  > Deploying systems on this data requires managing complex phenomena such as overlapping speech, heterogeneous accents, and ambient noise.
- `evaluation_method` = model-derived-metric, reference-metric, human-expert-eval, statistical-fit · [S3][iwslt-s3]
  - why: COMET ranks the offline track and is the score the compression track reports (COMET-XL is the simultaneous track's quality metric), and the African/Celtic speech-to-speech score and voice cloning's speaker similarity come from ASR and ECAPA-TDNN models, all model-derived. BLEU, chrF++, TER, characTER and SubER are reported beside them and rank the low-resource and subtitling tracks. Professional translators give direct assessment scores to the primary runs of the offline, compression and instruction-following tracks. The metrics track is scored by Kendall's tau-b correlation with human judgements.
  > the submitted runs will be ranked based on COMET calculated on the test set by using automatic resegmentation of the hypothesis based on the reference translation by mwerSegmenter
- `designed_for_subjects` = task-specific-supervised-model, instruction-tuned-model, generative-media-model · [S3][iwslt-s3]
  - why: The offline, low-resource, simultaneous and subtitling tracks are built for trained speech translation systems, cascades and end-to-end models alike. The instruction-following track is built for speech language models prompted with a task instruction, and the speech-to-speech and voice-cloning tracks score the speech a system generates.
  > Both cascade and end-to-end models will be evaluated.
- `secondary_axes` = latency · [S4][iwslt-s4]
  - why: The simultaneous track scores every system for latency beside quality.
  > For latency, we report LongYAAL as the primary metric

Considered and rejected:

- `capability` not `instruction-following` · [S4][iwslt-s4]
  - why: The instruction-following track gives a task instruction with the audio, but each task's output is scored for correctness (WER, COMET, BERTScore), not for whether the stated direction was obeyed apart from the content.
  > The model receives both a speech input and a task instruction in textual form and is expected to follow the instruction to produce the appropriate output.
- `evaluation_method` not `human-crowd-eval` · [S4][iwslt-s4]
  - why: The direct-assessment raters are professional translators, which is human-expert-eval.
  > Annotation is conducted by professional translators fluent in the source language and native in the target language.

- [ ] Identity and id: the name, aliases, id, paper and release date are right, and this is one benchmark, not a family or an edition of another

- [ ] Task and evaluation: the task, scoring, ground truth, entrants and harness read as the sources describe them
- [ ] Data and licence: access, refresh, provenance, sizes, subsets, contamination and licences match the sources

### 2.6 MIREX (mirex)

`data/benchmarks/audio-speech/mirex.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-10-14 · last verified 2026-11-18

*ISMIR's yearly music information retrieval evaluation since 2005, from chord and beat tasks to music generation.*

The Music Information Retrieval Evaluation eXchange, a yearly community evaluation campaign held with the ISMIR conference since 2005. Each edition is a set of tasks, each led by a task captain who defines it, collects the submissions, runs or scores them and publishes a results page on the MIREX wiki. Music audio is copyrighted, so MIREX has worked algorithm-to-data: participants submit their algorithms and the organisers run them on test collections that are not distributed. IMIRSEL at the University of Illinois ran it from 2005 to 2021 and had evaluated 1,997 algorithms on 37 test collections by 2013. No edition ran in 2022 or 2023; a Future MIREX team revived it in 2024 with a new submission site, docker submissions and generative tasks. The 2026 edition lists fourteen tasks: six standardized evaluation suites whose scoring code is public (chord, beat, key and downbeat estimation, music structure analysis and lyrics-to-audio alignment), lyrics transcription, instrument recognition, audio-to-score transcription, performance difficulty prediction, music evaluation on CMI-RewardBench, rhythm game chart generation, and symbolic and audio music generation judged by listening tests.

**Evidence** (52 quoted fields), by checklist area:

#### mirex · Identity and id

- `self_description` · [S1][mirex-s1]
  > MIREX (Music Information Retrieval Evaluation eXchange) is an annual community evaluation campaign held in conjunction with the International Society for Music Information Retrieval Conference
- `released` = null · [S2][mirex-s2]
  > MIREX officially began in 2005 and had its first plenary and poster sessions in ISMIR 2005

#### mirex · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary audio-speech/music-understanding; secondary audio-speech/music-generation; per_edition true · [S3][mirex-s3]
  - why: Most tasks in every edition take a music recording and score the musical attributes recovered from it -- chords, beats, downbeats, keys, structure, instruments, lyrics. Since 2024 the symbolic and audio music generation tasks score generated music, the secondary leaf; each carries its own domain in subsets.
  > This task requires participants to extract or transcribe a sequence of chords from an audio music recording.
- `capability` = perception · [S3][mirex-s3]
  - why: The understanding tasks take a music recording and score what was recovered from it, for chords the labels and their times against human annotations, weighted by song length.
  > This final number is referred to as the weighted chord symbol recall (WCSR).
- `evaluation_method` = domain-metric, human-crowd-eval, human-expert-eval · [S3][mirex-s3]
  - why: The understanding tasks are scored with MIR's own measures, for chords the chord symbol recall under five chord vocabularies beside a directional Hamming segmentation score. The generation tasks are judged by listening tests, in 2025 Symbolic Music Generation by 20 listeners of diverse music backgrounds, in 2026 Music Audio Generation by three trained evaluators (see subsets).
  > MIREX typically uses chord symbol recall (CSR) to estimate how well the predicted chords match the ground truth
- `designed_for_subjects` = task-specific-supervised-model, generative-media-model · [S3][mirex-s3]
  - why: The entrants are models trained for one task -- the 2026 chord task makes learned submissions ship their trained models, and the 2025 entrants include a Mamba-based chord recogniser -- and, since 2024, music generators whose generated music is what the listeners score.
  > Submissions using machine learning models must also submit their trained models.

Considered and rejected:

- `domain` not `multimodal/audio-language` · [S4][mirex-s4]
  - why: The 2024 and 2025 editions ran Music Description & Captioning, and 2025 Music Reasoning QA, which pair music audio with text. Neither is in the 2026 lineup, and they were two of 2025's thirteen tasks.
  > 2025:Music Description & Captioning
- `designed_for_subjects` not `classical-algorithm` · [S5][mirex-s5]
  - why: The 2025 chord task ran Chordino (NNLS Chroma) as a baseline, but the sources read do not say whether it has a learned component, and every entrant named there is a learned model.
  > Baseline: Chordino NNLS Chroma v1.1

#### mirex · Task and evaluation

- `learned_entrant_evidence` = system BMACE (a Mamba-based chord recogniser, 2025 Audio Chord Estimation) · [S5][mirex-s5]
  > BMACE A Mamba-Based Model for Automatic Chord Recognition
- `reproducible_by_third_party` = false · [S2][mirex-s2]
  - why: The test audio is copyrighted and not distributed, and the 2025 chord task's main sets include Yamaha's private collections, so only the organisers can produce the official numbers. The scoring code and the labels of public sets are released.
  > prevents researchers from replicating the evaluation and benchmarking their newly developed algorithms on their own
- `task` = exists true; input a music recording, given to the submitted program by the organisers, for the understanding tasks, for Symbolic Music Generation a 4-measure piano prompt as a note list; for Music Audio Generation a full-length source song and a style or arrangement prompt; output Per task -- timed chord labels and the other musical attributes the task names (beats, downbeats, keys, structure, instruments, lyrics and their alignment, a score); a 12-measure piano continuation; a complete cover-song recording.; scoring Each task on its own metrics over its own test sets, published per test set on the task's results page. Chord estimation is scored by weighted chord symbol recall under five vocabularies and by segmentation; the generation tasks by mean listener ratings on 5-point scales. · [S3][mirex-s3]
  > This task requires participants to extract or transcribe a sequence of chords from an audio music recording.
- `execution.compute_tier` = provided-allocation · [S3][mirex-s3]
  - why: For the standardized suites the organisers run every submitted image on their own GPU server, so the entrant pays for training only. Music Audio Generation 2026 is the exception, where teams run their own systems.
  > \[withheld: it may name a person; see the entry file\]
- `execution.reproducibility_tier` = not-independently-reproducible · [S2][mirex-s2]
  - why: The headline numbers need test audio and private labels only the organisers hold, and the generation tasks' numbers need their listening panels.
  > the test data used in MIREX cannot be distributed to participants
- `execution.harness` = mirex-evaluation (python main.py with the task name, for the standardized suites) · [S9][mirex-s9]
  > This is the open-source repo for all tasks evaluated by MIREX.
- `aggregation_policy` = none-by-design · [S1][mirex-s1]
  - why: Each task captain scores the task and publishes its own results page; no source combines tasks into one ranking.
  > Report results to MIREX and create a results page on the MIREX Wiki.

### 2.7 DCASE Challenge (dcase)

`data/benchmarks/audio-speech/dcase.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-10-14 · last verified 2026-11-19

*Yearly IEEE AASP challenge on sound scene and event analysis since 2013; independent tasks scored by their organisers.*

The yearly challenge of the DCASE community on the automatic analysis of everyday sound, held as an IEEE AASP challenge in 2013 and every year since 2016, with its results presented at the DCASE Workshop. Each edition is a set of independent tasks that the DCASE Steering Group selects from proposals; each task's organising team publishes development data and a baseline in the spring, releases the evaluation audio without labels about two weeks before the deadline, and scores the system outputs that participants submit. Every submission must include a technical report, and each task is ranked on its own metric, with no ranking across tasks. Acoustic scene classification was Task 1 in all eleven editions up to 2025, beside sound event detection, sound event localization and detection (from 2019), anomalous sound detection for machine condition monitoring (from 2020), bioacoustics, audio tagging, audio captioning and language-based audio retrieval. The 2026 edition had seven tasks: heterogeneous audio classification, noise-aware anomalous sound detection, semantic acoustic imaging for sound event localization and detection, spatial semantic segmentation of sound scenes, audio-dependent question answering, audio moment retrieval from long audio, and domain-incremental audio classification. It received 421 entries from 135 teams, and its results were published at the end of June.

**Evidence** (111 quoted fields), by checklist area:

#### dcase · Identity and id

- `self_description` · [S1][dcase-s1]
  > DCASE is a data challenge whose purpose is to produce new scientific knowledge about methods for detection and classification of sound scenes and events.
- `released` = 2013-03-31 · [S2][dcase-s2]
  > The first DCASE challenge campaign was organized between 31st March 2013 - 14th April 2013.

#### dcase · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary audio-speech/audio-event-understanding; secondary audio-speech/audio-event-detection-localization, audio-speech/machine-condition-monitoring, audio-speech/bioacoustics, multimodal/audio-language, multimodal/cross-modal-retrieval; per_edition true · [S3][dcase-s3]
  - why: Classifying sounds is the challenge's one continuous line. Acoustic scene classification was Task 1 in every edition from 2013 to 2025, and in 2026 heterogeneous audio classification (Task 1) and domain-incremental audio classification (Task 7) both score which sound class a recording holds. Detection and localization, machine condition monitoring, bioacoustics and the audio-language tasks are secondary, each the leaf of some editions' tasks.
  > In a way, this task replaces the former Task 1 on Acoustic Scene Classification, which ran for all 11 previous DCASE Challenge editions with different focuses every year
- `capability` = perception · [S4][dcase-s4]
  - why: Every task takes audio, from single clips to four-channel spatial recordings and minutes-long recordings, and scores what was recovered from it.
  > However, a significant amount of research is still needed to reliably recognize sound scenes and individual sound sources in realistic soundscapes
- `capability` = distribution-shift-generalization · [S5][dcase-s5]
  - why: Task 2 scores its source and target domains separately, the target domain differing in operating speed, load, noise and signal-to-noise ratio, and its evaluation machine types are not the development ones; the task, normal against anomalous, is unchanged.
  > Also, in order to evaluate the detection performance for each domain, the AUC is calculated for each domain.
- `capability` = continual-learning · [S6][dcase-s6]
  - why: Task 7 reveals three domains in sequence without access to earlier data and ranks by accuracy averaged over all three, so forgetting an earlier domain costs score.
  > The accuracy will be calculated separately for each domain, then overall accuracy will be calculated as the average over the three domains.
- `capability` = grounding · [S4][dcase-s4]
  - why: Task 6 scores whether a free-form text query was attached to the right stretch of a long recording.
  > Audio moment retrieval is the task of retrieving specific moments within long audio recordings that align with a given textual query.
- `capability` = temporal-reasoning · [S7][dcase-s7]
  - why: Task 6's answer is a start and an end time, correct only when its overlap with the reference moment reaches the IoU threshold (0.7 for the ranking), so the score depends on when the sound happened and how long it lasted.
  > A predicted moment is regarded as correct when its IoU with a reference moment is at least a threshold
- `evaluation_method` = classification-metric, domain-metric, multiple-choice, statistical-fit, composite, entrant-relative-ranking · [S8][dcase-s8]
  - why: Each task keeps its own ranking metric; Task 3's, quoted, is a cumulative rank over two metrics of different methods, so it depends on who else entered.
  > Overall ranking will be based on the cumulative rank of the metrics mentioned above, sorted in ascending order.
- `designed_for_subjects` = task-specific-supervised-model, instruction-tuned-model · [S9][dcase-s9]
  - why: Most tasks are built for audio models trained on the task's development data and scored as trained, the field's general audio tasks rather than a scientific discipline's. Task 5 alone is for large audio-language models prompted with each multiple-choice question, and admits only open-source ones.
  > Only open-source Large Audio Language Models are permitted for the audio understanding system submitted for evaluation.

#### dcase · Governance and independence

- `governance.maintainer` = The DCASE Steering Group, with each edition's task organising teams (an IEEE AASP challenge) · [S1][dcase-s1]
  - why: The Steering Group selects the tasks and sets the schedule; each task's team produces its data, scores its submissions and presents its results at the DCASE Workshop.
  > DCASE consists of independent tasks organized by teams who are, within the schedule defined by the DCASE Steering Group, responsible for producing the required data and instructions for participation, scoring the task submissions, providing a summary of the results, and presenting the results at the DCASE Workshop.
- `governance.submission_process` = held-out-server, publication-gated · [S11][dcase-s11]
  > Challenge submission consists of a submission package (one zip package) containing system outputs, system meta information, and technical report (pdf file).
- `governance.independence_flags` = flag maintainer-competes-on-own-benchmark · [S8][dcase-s8]
  > \[withheld: it may name a person; see the entry file\]

#### dcase · Lifecycle and activity

- `lifecycle` = active · [S4][dcase-s4]
  - why: The 2026 edition ran from April to June, ranked 421 entries and published its results; its workshop was held in Boston on 28-29 October 2026, with the task description papers in its proceedings (Zenodo, 2026-10-27, src-zenodo-22954971), and the 2027 edition has been called.
  > DCASE2026 Challenge received 421 submission entries
- `activity` = round-scheduled · [S1][dcase-s1]
  - why: The 2026 results are out and no round is open, but the call for the 2027 edition, posted on 1 October 2026, dates its opening.
  > 1 April 2027 Challenge opening: datasets and baseline methods published
- `events` = name DCASE2026 Workshop, Boston, 28-29 October 2026; kind workshop · [S10][dcase-s10]
  > The 11th Workshop on Detection and Classification of Acoustic Scenes and Events, DCASE 2026, will be held in Boston on 28-29 October.
- `versions` = 12 items · [S1][dcase-s1]
  - why: Each edition is a new evaluation, so every edition is a breaking version and no score is compared across years. Its tasks are chosen afresh, its schedule releases an evaluation set of its own without labels two weeks before the deadline (1 June 2026 for 2026; the call for 2027 sets the same), and it ranks only its own entries. A result names one edition and one task-and-year subset of it (dcase@2025 with dcase#2025-task1), never the family, and the comparability key carries the version. The one reuse read, 2026 Task 3 scoring DCASE2024's evaluation audio with new labels, is its own ranking and is not comparable with 2024's Task 3 either.
  > 1 April 2027 Challenge opening: datasets and baseline methods published 1 June 2027 Evaluation set release

**Open review checks** (15):

1. (field `comparability`) The comparability profile table maps statistical-fit with instruction-tuned-model to forecasting, so Task 3's Pearson r makes lead\_time and resolution\_window material, though no DCASE task forecasts. ADR-0024 (D3) removes entry-level waivers of those two fields and puts the fix in the profile rule; whether that pair should map to forecasting is the open question.
2. (field `versions`) Identity. The entry is the challenge as one family, with yearly editions as versions and every task of every edition as a task-and-year subset. Long-running task lines (anomalous sound detection since 2020, sound event localization and detection since 2019) could instead be entries of their own. A subset is tied to its edition only by its id (dcase#2025-task1 under version 2025), because the Subset model has no version field; the tie is held by tests/test\_dcase\_open\_asr.py, not by the schema.
3. (field `domain`) The primary domain is audio-event-understanding because scene and sound classification is the one line in every edition, but scene classification is not strictly the leaf's case (which sound events are present), and sound event detection ran in ten of twelve editions. audio-event-detection-localization could be argued as primary. · [S3][dcase-s3]
   > In a way, this task replaces the former Task 1 on Acoustic Scene Classification, which ran for all 11 previous DCASE Challenge editions with different focuses every year
4. (field `activity`) activity round-scheduled rests on the 2027 call's tentative schedule (posted 1 October 2026). governance.yaml and lifecycle.yaml cite dcase-2026 as between-rounds, written before the call; between-rounds holds if a tentative date is not an announced one. · [S1][dcase-s1]
   > 1 April 2027 Challenge opening: datasets and baseline methods published
5. (field `governance.submission_process`) publication-gated rests on the technical report being part of every submission package; no 2026 source states that a submission without one is unranked (the general rules page, challenge2026/rules, returned 404). · [S11][dcase-s11]
   > Challenge submission consists of a submission package (one zip package) containing system outputs, system meta information, and technical report (pdf file).
6. (field `governance.independence_flags`) maintainer-competes-on-own-benchmark rests on organisers of one task entering another (a Task 5 organiser at CUHK, in Task 3) and on ranked organiser baselines, not on the Steering Group entering a system. Whether the industry organisers' own teams entered their tasks was not checked, and the workshop's sponsors were not read. · [S8][dcase-s8]
   > \[withheld: it may name a person; see the entry file\]
7. (field `capability`) temporal-reasoning rests on Task 6's IoU-thresholded start and end times; no 2026 task scores onsets and offsets of a closed class set, which earlier sound event detection tasks did.
8. (field `evaluation_method`) Task 7's accuracy is the mean of class-wise accuracies, tagged classification-metric as a macro-averaged accuracy; Stage 3 tagged it exact-match. · [S6][dcase-s6]
   > Domain-wise accuracy will be calculated as average of the class-wise accuracies.
9. (field `designed_for_subjects`) instruction-tuned-model is tagged for Task 5 alone, whose open-source audio-language entrants are prompted with each question but often fine-tuned on its training set first.
10. (field `data.access`) data.access and the reproducibility tier assume the 2026 evaluation labels are withheld; only Task 2's release was read. If most tasks have published theirs, fully-open and fully-automatable may fit completed editions. · [S12][dcase-s12]
   > Ground truth of the normal and anomaly labels
11. (field `subsets`) Task 4 has no domain\_override; its score joins detection of which classes are present with separation, for which no audio-speech leaf exists.
12. (field `subsets`) The 2026 subsets rest on the task pages and, for Task 6, its overview paper. The proceedings (src-zenodo-22954971) hold the description papers of Tasks 1, 2, 4, 5, 6 and 7, and arXiv carries task overviews for Tasks 2, 4, 5 and 7 (2606.01578, 2604.00776, 2607.18718, 2606.02173, per the 2026-11-17 sweep). Neither the volume's PDF nor those four papers were read; they could confirm or correct the subsets' notes and item counts. · [S15][dcase-s15]
   > This volume is a collection of the papers presented at the Detection and Classification of Acoustic Scenes and Events 2026Workshop (DCASE 2026)
13. (field `subsets`) The 61 subsets from 2013 to 2025 rest on the events page's task lists alone. Their leaves and capabilities come from the task names, and no task page before 2026 was read, so none records a metric, an item count or a track. Two-part task lines (2013 Task 2, 2022 and 2023 Task 6, 2023 Task 4) are not split into children; the two sound-synthesis tasks inherit the family's domain for want of a leaf, and 2024 Task 10 (traffic monitoring) gets no leaf from its name. · [S14][dcase-s14]
   > Task 6, Automated Audio Captioning and Language-Based Audio Retrieval Task 7, Foley Sound Synthesis
14. (field `capability`) The earlier subsets carry perception alone where their names leave more open. The sound event detection tasks may score onsets and offsets (temporal-reasoning, which the family tags from 2026 Task 6 alone); the first-shot anomalous sound tasks of 2023 to 2025 may score shifted domains, as 2026's does; the few-shot bioacoustic tasks may fix a small support set (sample-efficiency, which is outside the family's list). None was tagged from a name alone.
15. (field `versions`) Cross-year comparison is refused because every edition is a breaking version and the comparability key carries the version and the task-and-year subset. That each edition's evaluation set is new rests on the 2026 and 2027 schedules and on the 2026 task pages; earlier editions' pages were not read. 2026 Task 3 scores DCASE2024's evaluation audio with new labels, so whether its ranking may sit beside 2024 Task 3's is open. · [S8][dcase-s8]
   > The evaluation dataset is identical to the one used in the DCASE2024 challenge.

**Reviewer checklist** for `dcase`:

- [ ] Identity and id: the name, aliases, id, paper and release date are right, and this is one benchmark, not a family or an edition of another
- [ ] Domain and capabilities: the primary and secondary subdomains, capabilities, evaluation methods and intended subjects fit, and no rejected term should have been kept

### 2.8 L3DAS Challenge (l3das)

`data/benchmarks/audio-speech/l3das.yaml` · `verification_status: ai-drafted-unverified` · curator confidence medium · added 2026-11-05 · last verified 2026-11-05

*Sapienza's challenge on 3D speech enhancement and sound event localization from dual Ambisonics recordings, 2021-2023.*

The challenge series of the L3DAS (Learning 3D Audio Sources) project at Sapienza University of Rome, run three times: L3DAS21 at IEEE MLSP 2021, then L3DAS22 and L3DAS23 as Signal Processing Grand Challenges at IEEE ICASSP 2022 and 2023. Every edition has the same two tasks on 8-channel audio from two first-order Ambisonics microphones 20 cm apart. Task 1, 3D speech enhancement, recovers the clean monophonic speech from a mixture with up to three office noises and is scored by (STOI + (1 - WER))/2, the WER taken from a pretrained Wav2Vec recogniser. Task 2, 3D sound event localization and detection, lists the active sounds of 14 office classes and their positions every 100 ms and is scored by a location-sensitive detection F-score (a true positive needs the right class within 2 m in 2022 and 1.75 m in 2023). L3DAS21 and L3DAS22 convolve Librispeech and FSD50K sounds with impulse responses measured in one real office; L3DAS23 moves to 68 simulated houses rendered with SoundSpaces 2.0 and adds an audio-visual track with a picture of each microphone's view. Each edition released labelled training and development data, then a blind test set without labels, and ranked the outputs that teams sent with a paper. The challenge drew 17 and 7 teams per task in 2022 and 4 and 2 in 2023; in 2024 the project held a paper special session at IJCNN instead of a challenge.

#### l3das · Domain and capabilities

- `domain` = primary audio-speech/audio-event-detection-localization; per_edition false · [S4][l3das-s4]
  - why: Task 2 scores when each sound is active (per 100-ms frame) and where it is (within a fixed Cartesian distance), which is the leaf's case, not merely which sounds are present. Task 1, speech enhancement, the other half of every edition, has no audio-speech leaf (logged with bench tag-gap), so the one leaf that fits a task of the series leads, and Task 1 keeps the family's root through the audio-speech inclusion test (the score is what was recovered from audio).
  > This metric considers a true positive only if a sound class is correctly predicted in a temporal frame and if it its predicted location lies within a cartesian distance from the true position of at most 1.75 m.
- `capability` = perception · [S5][l3das-s5]
  - why: Both tasks take raw 8-channel Ambisonics audio and score what was recovered from it, a clean speech waveform or the class and position of each active sound.
  > This metric measures the Cartesian distance between the predicted and true events and only considers a true positive when the label is correct and the location is within a threshold (1.75 m) of the reference location.
- `evaluation_method` = domain-metric, model-derived-metric, composite, classification-metric · [S5][l3das-s5]
  - why: The WER in Task 1's metric comes from a fixed pretrained recogniser, and the metric averages it with STOI.
  > We use a Wav2Vec architecture pre-trained on Librispeech 960h to compute the WER.
- `designed_for_subjects` = task-specific-supervised-model · [S6][l3das-s6]
  - why: Entrants are enhancement and SELD networks trained on the edition's training data and scored as trained; the baselines are a beamforming U-Net and an augmented SELDNet. An enhancement network reproducing a reference signal is this term rather than generative-media-model.
  > For task 1 we use a Beamforming U-Net and for task 2 an augmented variant of the SELDNet architecture.

Task 1 (speech enhancement) has no leaf, and on participation (17 and 4 teams against 7 and 2) and later use it is the larger half of the series. If a speech-enhancement leaf is added (the tag-gap record proposes one), it may deserve the primary, with SELD secondary. · [S11][l3das-s11]

If development-set use does not count as results on the instrument, mature fits (a formally ended competition keeps the instrument's standing). · [S7][l3das-s7]

4. (field `lineage`) Difference from DCASE's SELD task (dcase.yaml, from 2019). L3DAS's SELD uses two first-order Ambisonics microphones 20 cm apart in one office (2021-2022) or simulated houses (2023), 14 office classes from FSD50K, positions in Cartesian or cylindrical coordinates with a distance threshold, and is paired with a speech enhancement task; DCASE's SELD runs on its own recorded spatial scenes, scored by DCASE's own metrics, and in 2026 became semantic acoustic imaging. The L3DAS22 paper credits DCASE2019 with introducing SELD. They are separate maintainers and data, so separate entries with no lineage link; a reviewer may want a related-to note. · [S11][l3das-s11]

5. (field `data.access`) Whether the blind test targets were ever released. The L3DAS22 paper says the blind set was "initially" released without targets; the Kaggle and Zenodo records read offer the test inputs only, and the 2026 paper scores on the development set. If the targets are public, data.access is fully-open after each edition and reproducibility becomes fully-automatable. · [S11][l3das-s11]
   > evaluation and was initially released with the only predictors data, without target labels/signals.
6. (field `evaluation_method`) L3DAS23 Task 2 ranks JLESS (T2 0.239) above NERCSLIP-USTC (T2 0.242), on the organisers' judgement of result quality beside the metric. The ranking is then partly an organiser judgement, which no evaluation\_method term records. · [S9][l3das-s9]
   > \* The quality of the results produced, as well as the T2 metric, was considered to define the ranking order.
7. (field `evaluation_method`) Task 2's metric is tagged classification-metric (an F-score). The location-sensitive detection metric is defined within the SELD literature, so domain-metric could be argued.
8. (field `data.size`) The Task 1 size. The L3DAS23 Task 1 page says "more than 4000" recordings while the paper says over 40,000 and about 90 hours; the paper's figure is used, and the page's is probably a dropped zero. · [S17][l3das-s17]
   > more than 4000 virtual 3D audio with a duration up to 12 seconds
9. (field `data.submission_limit`) submission\_limit is one set of results per participant per edition, read from the rule that no one may join two teams; a team could replace its submission before the deadline. · [S12][l3das-s12]
   > each new submission will replace the one(s) previously made
10. (field `versions`) L3DAS21 results were found for Task 1 only (two teams); the MLSP 2021 results page lists no Task 2 ranking, and the L3DAS21 Task 2 outcome was not established. · [S18][l3das-s18]
   > Metric: 0.8651 WER: 0.1558 STOI: 0.8860
